extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and platform designers interested in peer review models and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing alternative peer-review models and platforms (e.g., GitHub, Wikipedia, Hypothesis, blockchain, ML-assisted) for scholarly publishing, including procedures, incentives, and quality-control mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply all code and data with submission
rubrics_metrics.description: As all code and data are supplied, peers would be able to assess methods and results comprehensively, which increases rigor, transparency, and replicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen in GitHub-style workflows where code and data accompany submissions; this enables reviewers to assess methods directly rather than relying solely on prose. Encourages reproducibility and reduces hidden-method risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifiability and credit for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: All parties are identified; reviewers would be able to claim credit and be acknowledged for their tracked contributions, and thereby quantify their impact on a project as a supply of individual prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GitHub/JOSS model tracks reviewer contributions; tracked contributions allow assessment of review quality and reviewer standing. Identification facilitates accountability and credit assignment; can be combined with reputational metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use version control for iterative, interactive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Version control facilitating interactive and dynamic evaluation in a post-publication environment, allowing fine-grained iteration between reviewers and authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Git-based workflows (e.g., GitHub issues) permit continuous updates, iterative fixes, and transparent history of changes. Supports post-publication amendments and a persistent review record linked to published submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured review check-lists of required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a review issue with a check-list of required elements for the review; reviewers perform their review by checking off elements of the review issue with which they are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by JOSS: check-lists guide reviewers and clarify acceptance criteria; allows iterative closure of items until all are resolved. Helps standardize minimal expectations and makes review progress visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host-neutral standards and prescribed directory structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop host-neutral standards (e.g., using a prescribed directory structure such as manuscript_version_1/peer_reviews) so peer review using Git is portable across hosts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages interoperability and archival stability; allows reviews and artifacts to be exchanged or migrated between platforms without losing structure or metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective moderation and community governance (Wikipedia-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation and quality control provided by a community of experienced editors and software-facilitated removal of mistakes; governance based on shared platform principles rather than personal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia demonstrates community-based quality control via volunteers and elected moderators. Governance structures (elections, norms) and software tools (edit conflict resolution) are necessary to maintain quality in an open system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, iterative 'peer production' rather than final-pass peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles never 'pass' a review; edits occur as cumulative and iterative improvements and so review is ongoing rather than a single gatekeeping event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia peer review is dynamic and continuous; lacks binary pass/fail outcomes. This model values contemporariness and continual improvement, which may be at odds with traditional accreditation models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity versus expert peer trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: A large inclusive volunteer pool can increase accessibility and readability but may lack subject-matter expertise, potentially propagating factual errors and creating perceptions of low quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia model: majority of volunteers often lack formal expertise; inviting subject-specific editors/WikiProjects can bring expertise. Consider combining inclusivity with trust metrics or expert invitations to mitigate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotations as user-controlled overlay (Hypothesis model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations belong to and are controlled by the user rather than any individual publisher or content host; annotations act as an overlay on top of static content and can be public, group-private, or private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis and similar services allow inline, precise annotations across formats (HTML, PDF). Annotations can be tied to ORCID and used during any stage (including preprints). Being overlay-based decouples review from publisher hosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotations enable collaborative reading/writing and post-publication audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations enrich research objects by adding knowledge, raising questions, collecting multiple perspectives, and enabling self-correction (e.g., PubPeer-led retractions; statcheck mass annotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotations can function as distributed post-publication peer review and fraud detection; they enable large-scale audits (statcheck) and focused critique (PubPeer). Recognition in scholarly reward systems remains limited but possible via ORCID linking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockchain for authentication and immutable provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchain can authenticate scientific papers using time stamps and checksums, providing irrevocable proof that a given manuscript existed on a date of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ledger and other blockchain projects use digital signatures and timestamps for proof-of-existence. Immutable records combat fraud and provide provenance for versions and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokenized incentivization and reputational rewards via blockchain
rubrics_metrics.description: A tokenized peer review system could reward contributors, reviewers, editors, and participants (e.g., 'Science Coins'); reviewers invest tokens in comments and are rewarded if contributions are upvoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens can remunerate or signal reputation, decouple identity from credit (allow anonymity while validating contributor status), and create economic incentives for quality reviewing. Requires careful protocol design to avoid gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blockchain to integrate broader publication functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Blockchains could potentially integrate data publication, research evaluation, incentivization, and research fund distribution into a single decentralized system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed uses include cohort-based training and proof-of-existence for trials. Uptake remains low and community unfamiliarity/concerns (e.g., association with cryptocurrencies) may limit adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated checks for minimal submission requirements (ML/text-mining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use automated tools to determine whether submitted work meets minimal requirements (e.g., clinical trial registration, consent statements, taxonomic name registration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text-mining tools (e.g., statcheck) and rule-based checks can reduce editorial burden by flagging missing mandatory items prior to human review. These are effective for procedural compliance checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated consistency/error detection (statistical and methodological checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated systems can scan for statistical errors or method-description incompleteness (e.g., check p-value correction declarations) and generate reports to assist human reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps surface obvious technical issues that should normally be checked manually. Can increase efficiency but should be used as an aid, not a sole determinant of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic reviewer recommendation and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatically determine the most appropriate reviewers for a manuscript using co-authorship networks, cognitive filtering, and social network weighting to reduce editor bias and identify conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such systems can widen potential referee pools and weight referees by prior contributions. Methods must mitigate bias risks and overfitting; reviewer weighting can include prior review experience and expertise signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive ML for assessing future impact (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning might predict future impact (e.g., citation counts) and be used as part of decision-making, but this risks increasing editorial selectivity and disadvantaging low-predicted-impact work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors should be cautious: predictive signals can bias selection toward 'popular' research and are better used as recommendations rather than replacement for human judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of ML: conformism and false positives
rubrics_metrics.description: ML and neural networks are largely considered to be conformist and can produce false positives, which may discourage submissions or mischaracterize novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer automation for recommendation and triage rather than final decisions. Monitor error modes (overfitting, false positives) and balance efficiency gains against risks to diversity and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of rigor for non-text scholarly products
rubrics_metrics.description: New forms of scholarship (digital humanities, visualizations, software, datasets) should 'be assessed with the same rigor used to judge scholarly quality in print media.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criteria must expand beyond prose to include community engagement, sustainability practices, reproducibility, and technical quality specific to the artifact type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software peer review must evaluate code and artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: For software outputs, both text and software should be reviewed; some journals (SoftwareX, JORS) review text and code equally, while JOSS focuses more on the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage submission of supporting material (code, artifacts). Use artifact evaluation committees or technical review tracks and offer badges/seals for successfully evaluated artifacts. GitHub workflows and issue-based reviews are practical mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data peer review: data availability and reviewer verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals ask authors to release data to reviewers and can ask reviewers to state whether they have reviewed the data themselves; the Peer Reviewers' Openness Initiative argues for all data being publicly available for evaluation and reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making data available helps detect errors, encourages good archiving standards, and incentivizes authors to validate analyses. Beware of reviewer overload — data checks add time and effort and require appropriate recognition/incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hybrid/multiple peer review models (series or parallel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple peer review models can be used in series or in parallel to iteratively improve documents (e.g., FORCE11 used GitHub, Hypothesis, and pre-publication review sequentially).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid approaches can combine strengths of different systems (open commenting, formal journal review, community annotation) and produce better outcomes; document provenance and summaries of reviews are useful adjuncts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize quality control, certification, and incentivization in hybrids
rubrics_metrics.description: Any modern peer review process or platform must harmonize the core non-independent features: quality control, certification, and incentivization, grounded in diverse community stakeholder engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should intentionally integrate mechanisms for ensuring content quality, clear certification/endorsement, and appropriate incentives (reputation, tokens, credit) to gain community buy-in and sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute review burden and enable task specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Making peer review a social process by distributing reviews to numerous peers divides the burden and allows individuals to focus on their particular area of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-network-like review systems (e.g., GitHub) let contributors pick tasks/repositories to follow; this leverages micro-expertise and can improve review coverage while reducing per-reviewer load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community attention/engagement as a quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential issue of proliferating non-significant work is minimal because projects not deemed interesting or of sufficient quality are simply never paid attention to in terms of follows, contributions, and re-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics such as follows, contributions, re-use, and upvotes can act as emergent quality filters in open systems, but designers must be cautious about popularity biases and ensure mechanisms to surface high-quality niche work.
